blocks.text: The gnats, although such insignificant creatures, were nevertheless created before man, so that he should not exalt himself in pride (Sanhedrin 38a); but precisely because of their insignificance, whoever eats them is an apostate from the Law, since he evidently ate the gnat not out of craving for pleasure but out of defiant wantonness (Horajoth 11a). On the fable of Titus's gnat see Gittin 56b, and on another fabulous statement of the Midrash about the gnat §. 519.
The Ethiopian gnat.
Sabbat 77b it is said that the lion is afraid of the creature מפניע. Rashi explains: מפניע is a small animal whose loud voice the lion fears because he believes it might be a large, strong animal.

But what מפניע itself is, Rashi does not explain. Bochart explains it as the Ethiopian gnat, which stings the eyes and the part of the lion's face bare of mane so painfully that the lion abandoned the whole region on account of this troublesome insect; he therefore fears even the buzzing of this gnat (Bochart: Hieroz. 2, 4, 17, col. 567 and ibid. 5, 18, col. 792).

Conclusion. The second part of Rashi's explanation (§. 433), however, rests on a truth of natural history; for the lion does indeed fear the thos (Θῶς [Thōs]; Arist. loc. cit. 9, 2, 11 and 9, 31, 4). According to Oppian (Hunting with Dogs 3, 336) the thos is the hybrid of the wolf and the female panther; it therefore cannot be [p. 317] as large as, or even larger than, the lion; more recent naturalists, on the other hand, would recognize in the thos the ounce (Felis onzo), cf. Mellin de Grandmaison in the „Journal de Physique (December 1787, num. 5); this is the jaguar, which is indeed of the size and strength of the lion (Voigt l. c. 1. p. 271). Its ferocity and dangerousness are well known.
The cattle horsefly.

Cattle were covered with a blanket to protect them from the זבובין (Para 2, 3), and nature gave them a long tail so that they could drive off the בקי; by these the cattle in the meadows are greatly tormented (Sabbat 77b). This is the Tabanus bovinus (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 258). Even now carriage horses are protected with nets against that insect, which stings cattle and horses dreadfully.
בקי is Arabic and denotes any bloodsucking insect (§. 432 and below p. 319).
The sheep botfly.

The female lays its eggs inside the nose of the sheep, which become restless when this happens. At the time of the strongest development of these insects, in spring and summer, they cause the staggers in sheep (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 276). The Talmud calls these botflies דרני ראשה „worms of the head“, i.e. in the head of the sheep, for the hatched larvae crawl upward into the frontal sinuses. The rams butt one another with their horns, whereby the larvae fall out; to the ewes one tied little chips of juniper (ריחמא; according to Rosenmüller loc. cit. 4, 2. p. 120: Ginther) before the nose, whereby they sneeze and expel those larvae (Sabbat 54b).
דרן is a collective name for several kinds of insects; see §§. 410, 437 and 444. R. Hai Gaon (Para 9, 2) identifies דרן with דירה (§. 413); on ריחמא and חנון see also above p. 120.
The cattle botfly.

Oestrus bovis. The larva of this genus lives under the skin of cattle and other animals, especially younger ones, no doubt [p. 318] because their hide is more easily pierced and they themselves are juicier (Voigt 5. p. 277). The Talmud calls these insects: דרני דבישרא „worms of the flesh“, which Rashi explains thus: תולעים הנמצאים בין עור לבשר כשמפשיטין הבהמה ובלע"ז גרביליש „worms which are found between the skin and the flesh of flayed cattle and are called גרבליש in the foreign language.“
On דרן see §. 436; the foreign word in Rashi is not known to me; in English our botfly is called Gad-Fly, which may perhaps facilitate identifying the Old French word.
The mayfly.

The only Talmudic passage (Chulin 58b) that deals with the mayfly must, to be understood, be quoted literally and in full. It reads: אמר רב ליה בקא בר יומא ולית דירבא בר שתא א"ל רב פפא לאביי והא אמרי אינשי שב שני אימרא בקחא [מבקא דאמרה ליה חזיתיה לבר מחוזא דסחה במיא וסלוק ואיכרך בסדינין ואותיבה עליה ומצית מיניה ולא הודעת לי] א"ל וליטעמך הא דאמרי אינשי שיתין מני דפרזלא תלו ליה לבקא בקורנסיה מי איכא איהו גופיה כמה הוי אלא במני דידהו הכי נמי בשני דידהו. According to Rashi the passage must be translated thus: „Rab said: „The Baka does not live a day, the fly not a year.““
Thereupon R. Papa said to Abaja: „But people relate that the female
Bakta
bore a grudge against the male
Baka
for seven years, for she reproached him: „You saw a man from Mechusa go down into the water and come out again; then you settled on him, sucked blood from him, and gave me no word of it.“
Abaja replied: „Have you not likewise heard the proverb: 60 pounds of iron were hung on the Baka's hammer (sting)? Is this possible? How big, then, is the Baka itself?
But just as the weight here is expressed figuratively, in proportion, so too is it the case with the years.““

Rashi misunderstood the word אימרא; he takes it in the sense of תמריא (Job 39, 10) and renders it as to resist; he says: לשון כעת תמריא נתנכרה לו ומרדה עליו אינשלבייר „similar to the biblical תמריא; the female acted as a stranger toward the male and was refractory toward him, the same as insoulever.“
